Name: Bozrah (Busra) (בוצרה (סוריה))
Description: A well in the northern part of the tel, dated to the Middle Bronze Age, which was abandoned along with a house and garden it supplied with water.

Name: Ebla (אבלה (סוריה))
Description: A very deep well in the lower city, connecting to a dome-roofed underground chamber, containing artifacts dated to around 2000 BCE.

Name: Jericho (יריחו)
Description: During the Middle Bronze Age, the city of Jericho was fortified, and Elisha's Spring (Ein es-Sultan) was intentionally included within its city walls to provide a secure water source.

Name: Jerusalem (City of David) (ירושלים (עיר דוד))
Description: The Gihon Spring was the primary water source for Jerusalem from the Chalcolithic period, and its abundant flow was seven times greater than the city's needs during the Middle Bronze Age. Channel I, a plastered channel partly cut into rock and partly built, is considered the oldest water system in the area, possibly dating to the Middle Bronze Age or earlier, used for irrigating agricultural plots in the Kidron Valley. The central water system of Jerusalem, including Warren's Shaft (tunnel part), the Great Tower, a pool, and Channels II and III, was carved and built during Middle Bronze Age II to provide the city with an internal water source, especially during sieges.

Name: Mari (מארי)
Description: Textual evidence from King Yahdun-Lim (18th century BCE) describes the construction of canals to bring water to Mari, potentially representing an early urban aqueduct, though no archaeological evidence has been found.

Name: Qatna (קטנה)
Description: During Middle Bronze Age II, a spring was enclosed within the walls of the kingdom city of Qatna, while a stream outside the rampart may have filled a moat for defense.

Name: Sha'albim (שעלבים)
Description: A burial cave from MB IIB was originally a rock-cut, mud-plastered water cistern, approximately 3m deep and 3m in diameter, with spiral steps for access.

Name: Tel Dan (תל דן)
Description: The city of Dan, enclosed by a massive rampart, incorporated the eastern springs of Dan within its fortifications during the Middle Bronze Age, serving as the primary water source. An artificial water passage (sinkhole) was likely constructed concurrently with the rampart to manage excess water.

Name: Tel Gerisa (תל גריסה)
Description: A water system consisting of an elliptical vertical shaft with steps, cut into the kurkar rock, was constructed during Middle Bronze Age IIA within the fortified city of Tel Gerisa to reach groundwater, likely for use during sieges.

Name: Tel Gezer (תל גזר)
Description: An impressive water system was discovered within the fortifications of Tel Gezer, comprising an entrance, a sloping tunnel with steps, a collection basin, and a cave, dating to the Middle Bronze Age. A large, complex stepped water tunnel, 40m long and nearly 40m deep, leading to a natural spring/groundwater source. The author argues for its construction in the Middle Bronze Age. Numerous bottle-shaped, rock-cut, and often plastered cisterns were found, typically 4.9-7m deep, with drainage channels collecting runoff. Specific examples like 23089 and 34046 are dated to the Middle Bronze Age, with some reused into later periods.

Name: Tel Haror (תל הרור)
Description: A 2m diameter, 11.5m deep well, lined with kurkar stones and rock-cut, located within the Middle Bronze Age city, intended to supply water during sieges. Dated by MB II pottery.

Name: Tel Hazor (תל חצור)
Description: A large depression in the lower city is suggested to be the top of a shaft dug to groundwater, used during the Middle Bronze and Late Bronze Ages. Six bottle-shaped, rock-cut cisterns (e.g., 9024, 9027, 6243) were found, dated to MB II by pottery, with some continuing into LB. They featured narrow necks, expanding bodies, and sometimes plaster, designed to collect rainwater runoff.

Name: Tel Kabri (תל כברי)
Description: A large planned city from MB II (c. 1800 BCE) was built around the abundant Ein Shefa spring, which was enclosed within the city's rampart. Excess water was likely drained through a channel in the western gate.

Name: Tel Lachish (תל לכיש)
Description: A 44m deep, 2.4m diameter cylindrical well, stone-lined and rock-cut, located within the city's Middle Bronze Age fortifications and used until the Iron Age.

Name: Tel Megiddo (תל מגידו)
Description: A large depression in the northern part of the tel is hypothesized to be an early water system (MB, LB, possibly EB) reaching groundwater, potentially connected to Ein el-Qubi.

Name: Tel Nami (תל נאמי)
Description: An unfortified settlement featured a rectangular/oval well, 2.3m deep, lined with fieldstones, dated to MB IIA. Its bottom is 1.2m below current sea level, indicating a lower sea level in the MB period.
